`event:india-smallcap-crash-2018` | confidence: **verified** | tags: india, blowup, smallcap, sector-nbfc, policy, base-rate

BSE Smallcap record high 20,183 on 15 Jan 2018 (Business Standard; another BS piece cites 18,672 on 14 Feb 2018 as the 52-week high - definitions differ); -23.5% in calendar 2018; ~-40% from Jan 2018 to Aug 2019 (Value Research). Smallcap 250 TRI -36% vs Nifty 50 TRI -14% (DSP drawdown table); intra-year fall of the Smallcap 100 ~40%. Meanwhile the Nifty kept making highs into Aug-Sept 2018 - a narrow market. Triggers: Oct 2017 SEBI MF recategorisation (fixed definitions of large/mid/small caps forced portfolio reshuffles), Feb 2018 budget reintroducing LTCG tax, the ASM surveillance framework (2018), the IL&FS default (Sept 2018; ~Rs 91,000 crore of debt, from memory), DHFL's ~60% intraday crash (21 Sept 2018) and an NBFC funding freeze; then 2019 governance blow-ups (DHFL, Yes Bank, Cox & Kings, CG Power). Leaders before: everything small, MF-flow beneficiaries; laggards: NBFCs/housing finance, autos, realty, promoter-pledged names. Winners during: large private banks, IT, consumer 'quality' (the 2019-20 quality premium peak). Recovery: ~3 years to regain the prior peak (DSP) - aided by the 2020 liquidity wave. Top signals: record SIP and small-cap fund inflows, breadth peaking (Jan 2018) while the index rose, IPO and QIP rush by small companies. Lesson: breadth divergence plus a credit event = small-cap bear market even if the Nifty looks fine.

|---|---|

| drawdown | ~-40% to Aug 2019; SC250 TRI -36% in 2018 |

**Formula (1968, public manufacturers).** Z = 1.2·X1 + 1.4·X2 + 3.3·X3 + 0.6·X4 + 1.0·X5
- X1 = working capital / total assets
- X2 = retained earnings / TA
- X3 = EBIT / TA
- X4 = market value of equity / total liabilities
- X5 = sales / TA

**Zones:**
- above 2.99: safe
- 1.81–2.99: grey
- below 1.81: distress
- For emerging-market or non-manufacturing firms use Z'' = 6.56X1 + 3.26X2 + 6.72X3 + 1.05X4 (book equity/TL). Distress is below 1.1 and safe is above 2.6.

**Data.** 10-K FY2024 (0000050863-25-000009), FY2025 (0000050863-26-000011). $ m.
- Market value is the cover-page public float (dei:EntityPublicFloat) at the end of Q2 of each fiscal year. It is a filing-sourced proxy that slightly understates market cap.
- Total liabilities = total assets − total equity including NCI.

| | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Current assets | 43,269 | 47,324 | 63,688 |
| Current liabilities | 28,053 | 35,666 | 31,575 |
| Total assets | 191,572 | 196,485 | 211,429 |
| Retained earnings | 69,156 | 49,032 | 48,983 |
| EBIT (operating income) | 93 | −11,678 | −2,214 |
| Public float (Jun of FY) | 140,000 | 132,400 | 99,300 |
| Total liabilities | 81,607 | 91,453 | 85,069 |
| Revenue | 54,228 | 53,101 | 52,853 |

**Steps for FY2024:**
- X1 = 11,658/196,485 = 0.0593, ×1.2 = 0.071
- X2 = 0.2495, ×1.4 = 0.349
- X3 = −0.0594, ×3.3 = −0.196
- X4 = 1.448, ×0.6 = 0.869
- X5 = 0.2703, ×1.0 = 0.270

Z = **1.36, the distress zone**. FY2023 was 1.91 (grey) and FY2025 was 1.42 (distress).

**What happened.**
- Intel did not default.
- In Aug-2025 the US government converted CHIPS Act grants into about 433 m new shares at $20.47 (a ~9.9% stake). SoftBank bought $2 bn of stock at $23, and Nvidia invested $5 bn.
- Shares outstanding went from 4.33 bn (FY24) to 4.99 bn (Jan-2026) to 5.32 bn (Oct-2026), about +23%.

**Lesson.** Z measures balance-sheet distress, not the outcome. For strategically important firms, "distress" often resolves through **dilution or a bail-in instead of bankruptcy**. Both outcomes are bad for existing equity. Z below 1.81 means "own only with a specific view on the recapitalisation".

**Hidden trap: Luckin's store and same-order growth** (`case_study:hidden-trap-luckin-growth`, verified). THE GOOD NUMBER: China's challenger to Starbucks reported hyper-growth in stores and revenue and improving unit margins, proof (it seemed) that subsidised growth was turning profitable; stock $17 IPO (May 2019) -> ~$50 (Jan 2020). WHY IT LIED: on 2 Apr 2020 Luckin admitted its COO fabricated ~RMB 2.2 bn ($310 m) of 2019 sales; shares -80% in a day; delisted Jun 2020. The improvement in 'store-level margins' was produced by the fake sales. TELLS: (1) Muddy Waters circulated an anonymous report based on ~11,000 hours of store video showing far fewer items per order than reported, an alt-data refutation of the reported unit economics; (2) chairman and founders had pledged most of their shares for margin loans; (3) follow-on equity and a convertible within months of IPO; (4) related-party history of the founding team. TEST: verify unit economics outside the company (receipts, footfall, app downloads, supplier volumes); treat insider margin loans plus rapid post-IPO capital raising as a governance flag. LESSON: unit-economics improvement is the most persuasive number in a loss-making growth company, so it is also the one worth faking. Contrast Eternal, where order volumes were checkable via restaurant partners and third-party data.

**Hidden trap: Valeant's 'cash EPS' growth from acquisitions** (`case_study:hidden-trap-valeant-eps-growth`, verified). THE GOOD NUMBER: Valeant reported fast-rising 'cash EPS' and revenue, run by a McKinsey-trained CEO who cut R&D to ~3% of sales; Pershing Square and Sequoia Fund owned it; the stock peaked ~$262 (Aug 2015). WHY IT LIED: (1) the growth was acquired, not organic: dozens of deals financed with ~$30 bn of debt (debt/EBITDA ~5-7x); (2) 'cash EPS' excluded acquisition and restructuring costs that recurred every year because buying companies was the business model; (3) revenue growth came from price increases (e.g., Syprine +3,000%) rather than volumes, inviting political backlash; (4) an undisclosed specialty pharmacy, Philidor, which Valeant had an option to buy, pushed its drugs. After Citron's Oct-2015 report and Philidor's exposure, the stock fell >90%; renamed Bausch Health. TEST: separate organic from acquired growth; add back 'one-time' costs that recur; check GAAP EPS and FCF after acquisitions; ask whether price or volume drives sales. Buffett's warning on high-P/E acquirers manufacturing EPS applies (insight:buffett-conglomerate-chain-letter-2014). LESSON: EPS growth that needs a continuous flow of debt-financed deals is a financing story, not a compounding business.

| Category | FY26 revenue ₹ mn [HSIE] | Mix FY26 | FY22–26 CAGR | Private label share | PL margin premium |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Apparel | 57,100 | 44.4% | 22.7% | ~100% ("fashion 100% own brand") | n/a |
| General merchandise | 36,802 | 28.6% | 22.2% | 73–74% | +300–400 bps vs national brands [HSIE] |
| FMCG | 34,804 | 27.0% | 25.4% | 35% of value, **60% of volume** | +10 pp [HSIE] |
| Total own brands | | **74.1%** FY26 (73.1% FY25); 72.5% Q2 FY27 [PPT-Q2] | | | |

- BRSR26 confirms the mix as 44/29/27. Q2 FY27 was 40.5/29.6/29.7 (the festive shift pulled apparel down).
- **Category gross margins are not disclosed. These are estimates.** Method: solve GM = Σ(mix × category GM) = 28.4%, with FMCG anchored at a DMart-like ~14–16% on national brands (VMM gets +10 pp on 35% of FMCG value, so FMCG ≈ 0.65×15% + 0.35×25% ≈ 18.5%). GM assumed at ~30–32%. That makes apparel ≈ (28.4 − 0.27×18.5 − 0.286×31)/0.444 ≈ **33–34%**. **Confidence: unverified.** Re-solve when any quarter gives a category GP.
- **Mix shift is the real gross-margin lever.** Opening price points fell from 60% of sales four years ago to 20% `[HSIE]`. Management says GM gains will be "reinvested in product quality". Read that as a stated **cap** on gross margin.
- Brand concentration: Brink (apparel) alone was about ₹1,000 cr in FY25 `[ELARA]`.
